headline.sentence: September, October and November alone bring in 37.2 percent of this wholesaler's revenue in the trailing twelve months (2010-12..2011-11) - half as much again as an evenly spread quarter would - and it is not a one-year artefact: the same three months were 36.1 percent of the year before (2009-12..2010-11). A one-line rule, 'this month equals the same month last year', predicts that peak quarter to within 5.9 percent.

drop_ledger.why: Sheets 'Year 2009-2010' and 'Year 2010-2011' both cover 2010-12-01 to 2010-12-09. Kept the sheet-1 copy, dropped the sheet-2 duplicate.
Identical Invoice+StockCode+Quantity+Price+timestamp+Country rows. Same line recorded twice; keeping both would double-count revenue.
Invoice numbers starting with 'C' are cancellations/returns with negative quantities. Excluded so the series measures gross sales.
Postage (POST/DOT), manual adjustments (M/ADJUST), bank charges, samples, Amazon fees, gift vouchers and TEST rows are not product sales.
Quantity <= 0 outside the credit-note set: write-offs and stock corrections, not sales.
Price <= 0 lines produce zero or negative revenue; they are freebies and entry errors, not sales.
The file stops on 2011-12-09, so December 2011 is a part-month and would read as a 58% collapse in a monthly series.

kept_deliberately: 243,007 rows with a missing Customer ID - valid transactions, only customer-level work would need the ID.
4,382 rows with a missing Description - the StockCode still identifies the product.

forecast.verdict: On the fixed 3-month holdout the regression edges the seasonal-naive baseline (5.49% vs 5.93% MAPE), but that is a 3-point comparison. On the 15-point rolling-origin backtest the baseline wins (6.38% vs 6.83%). The honest reading is that the regression does not reliably beat 'same month last year' on this series.

claim_check.real_value: 40,774 clean records per month (978,583 over 24 months)
claim_check.note: Comfortably clears 15K. The claim understates the dataset by roughly 2.7x, which is the good kind of error.

The file has a single free-text Country field. The four geography buckets on the dashboard (UK / Ireland / Rest of Europe / Rest of World) are defined in pipeline.py by us, not read from the data. The bullet should say so.

claim_check.real_value: 4,893 distinct stock codes; the top 12 are only 8.36% of revenue
claim_check.note: The dashboard does show 12 products, but they are the twelve largest of nearly five thousand and they account for under a tenth of turnover. Describing the catalogue as 12 products is wrong by two orders of magnitude.

claim_check.resume_claim: Used pivot tables, VLOOKUP, conditional formatting and charts
claim_check.real_value: VLOOKUP, conditional formatting and native charts are in the workbook. There are no PivotTables.
claim_check.note: openpyxl cannot emit a pivotCache/pivotTable part, so the pivot logic is done with SUMIFS over a tidy fact table - same cross-tab, recalculates live, no manual refresh. Claiming PivotTables would be false and is not claimed.

claim_check.resume_claim: linear regression to forecast next-quarter sales with 93% accuracy
claim_check.real_value: MAPE 5.49% on the held-out quarter (= 94.51% 'accuracy'), RMSE GBP 89,466, R2 0.765 on n=3 months
claim_check.note: '93% accuracy' is not a defined regression metric. Translated to MAPE, the number is roughly right - forecasts landed within about 5% of actual on the held-out quarter. But the claim is hollow without a baseline: a one-line seasonal-naive rule scores 5.93%, and on a 15-point rolling-origin backtest the baseline actually wins (6.38% vs 6.83%). The regression does not reliably beat 'same month last year'.

claim_check.real_value: no inventory, stock-out or fulfilment field exists in this dataset
claim_check.note: A downstream business outcome that no public transaction file can evidence. Kept off the site. The defensible inventory-relevant fact is the seasonality: 37.2% of the trailing twelve months' revenue lands in September-November.

dashboard_no_xlookup.detail: XLOOKUP needs an _xlfn prefix through openpyxl and would render #NAME?

forecast_predicts_with_trend.detail: 24 TREND formulas (prediction does not depend on LINEST coefficient ordering)

forecast_holdout_not_in_training.detail: every TREND known_y stops at row 26, so the held-out months never enter the fit

workbook_design_matrix_reproduces_python.detail: max abs difference GBP 0.000000 between the sheet's own design matrix refitted and the published forecast

data_is_values_not_formulas.detail: source facts are literal values, as they should be

excel.pivottables: none - openpyxl cannot write a pivotCache part; SUMIFS over a tidy fact table is used instead

caveats: 24 complete months is the bare minimum for a seasonal forecast: each calendar month is observed exactly twice, so every seasonal coefficient rests on two data points.
The two source worksheets overlap for 2010-12-01 to 2010-12-09. Analyses that concatenate them without deduplicating double-count 22,523 rows and report a false December 2010 spike.
December 2011 is truncated on the 9th and is excluded; the series ends 2011-11.
'Region' is not in the data. The four geography buckets are ours, built from the 43-value free-text Country column.
This is one UK online gift wholesaler in 2009-2011. Nothing here generalises to other retailers or to today.
No LibreOffice or Excel is installed on the build machine, so the workbook is verified structurally (zip CRC, XML well-formedness, relationship resolution, openpyxl reload) rather than by opening it.
